subject: What Changed to Your Credit Card Today? Edition 15
summary: IDFC FIRST Bank drops forex markup to zero across fourteen cards but ends reward points on international spends from 26 October, Axis Bank adds six new 1% fees to its REWARDS card, and HDFC halves the income bar on its IRCTC card.
body_html:
What Changed to Your Credit Card Today?

Edition 15, 9 September 2026

If you carry an IDFC FIRST Bank credit card, today's edition is basically about you. The bank quietly rewrote the international-spending fine print on fourteen of its cards in one sweep, and every single one of them points to the same trade: zero forex markup starting today, in exchange for reward points on your foreign spends disappearing from 26 October 2026. That is a real trade, not a freebie, and we are going to work out exactly what it saves you and what it costs you, card by card. Alongside that, Axis Bank bolted six new 1% fees onto one of its most-used cards, HDFC quietly made a travel co-brand card easier to qualify for, and Kotak trimmed two more cards. None of this comes with a bank press release; it is what their own pages show today, so read the honest-caution note on each item before you act.

Axis Bank REWARDS Credit Card

This is the same card that lost its purchase protection, credit shield, and travel insurance covers back in Edition 8 on 27 August. Today it picked up six new 1% transaction fees: rent payments, wallet loads once your cumulative load crosses ₹10,000 in a cycle, fuel spends once cumulative fuel crosses ₹50,000 in a cycle, education payments made through third-party apps, utility bills once cumulative utility crosses ₹25,000 in a cycle, and online skill-gaming spends once cumulative gaming crosses ₹10,000 in a cycle.

Here is what that actually costs you. Pay ₹20,000 rent through this card every month, and the new 1% fee takes ₹200 a month, ₹2,400 a year, straight off the top, before you even count the platform's own rent-payment charge. Top up a wallet like Paytm or PhonePe with ₹12,000 in a month, and because this fee triggers on the whole cumulative amount once you cross ₹10,000, you pay ₹120 that cycle, not just 1% on the ₹2,000 above the threshold.

The catch: this is unverified, taken only from the bank's own page; we have not found independent confirmation it is live yet, so check your next statement closely.

What I'd do: if rent or wallet loads are a big part of why you use this card, run your last three statements against your reward rate. If the new 1% fee eats more than the rewards you earn on that spend, move that specific payment to a card that does not charge it yet, most mid-tier HDFC and ICICI cashback cards still don't.

HDFC Bank IRCTC Credit Card

The minimum monthly income requirement for new applicants has dropped from ₹25,000 to ₹12,000. That roughly doubles the pool of salaried Indians who clear the bar on paper, opening the door to first-jobbers and smaller-town earners who were locked out before.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page, no press release yet, and a lower income bar never guarantees approval; your CIBIL score and existing credit exposure still decide the outcome.

What I'd do: if you or someone in your family earns between ₹12,000 and ₹25,000 a month and travels by train often, this card is now worth applying for. Its real value, IRCTC-specific rewards and railway lounge access, doesn't change with the income tier you qualify under.

Kotak Royale Signature Credit Card

This card is already closed to new applicants; Kotak marks it Discontinued on its own site. But existing holders' reward structure just got thinner. International spends have been dropped from the accelerated 4-points-per-₹150 category and now earn only the base 2-points-per-₹150 rate.

Spend ₹1 lakh on an overseas trip: at the old 4X rate that was roughly 2,667 points, at the new base rate it's roughly 1,333 points, a loss of about 1,334 points on that one trip. At Kotak's typical redemption value of around ₹0.50 a point, that's close to ₹667 gone on a single lakh of foreign spend, more if you travel more.

The catch: unverified from the bank's own page.

What I'd do: if you still hold this card and travel abroad, route that specific spend to a card that still rewards international transactions properly, keep this one for its India-focused perks instead.

Kotak Cashback+ Credit Card

The minimum cashback redemption threshold is rising from 100 points to 500 points, effective 16 October 2026. Since 1 point equals ₹1, the ₹100 sitting as redeemable cashback today won't be redeemable that way after 16 October; you'll need to let it build to ₹500 first.

If your typical monthly spend on this card earns ₹150 to ₹200 in cashback, you could redeem almost every cycle before this change. After 16 October, expect to wait closer to three months before you can touch it.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: nothing changes about how you spend, but stop expecting quick top-ups against your bill; plan to let cashback build up for a quarter before redeeming.

FIRST Millennia: the forex trade behind today's IDFC FIRST sweep

IDFC FIRST rewrote the forex section across its card portfolio today, and FIRST Millennia's page shows the clearest version of the new deal. Zero Forex Markup is now front and centre, and buried in the fine print, repeated three times on the page, is this line: "Effective 26th October 2026, international transactions will not earn Reward Points."

Here's the mechanism in plain terms. Zero forex markup means the 3 to 3.5% conversion fee most cards quietly charge on foreign-currency spends doesn't apply here; that part is a genuine saving, today, not in October. But starting 26 October, whatever you spend abroad, or on any international website from India, earns zero reward points on this card. The card's birthday 10X bonus category is also being reworded to drop "international purchases" from at least one part of the page.

The math: say you spend ₹2 lakh a year on international transactions, a mix of travel and online shopping. At the card's base rate of roughly 1 point per ₹150, that's about 1,333 points a year, worth somewhere between ₹270 and ₹530 depending on how you redeem. Skip a 3% forex markup on the same ₹2 lakh and you save about ₹6,000. In pure rupees, the zero-markup saving is worth far more than the points you lose, but it's still a real benefit quietly disappearing, not something to wave away as "free."

The catch: unverified from the bank's own page; we haven't found independent confirmation the 26 October date holds.

What I'd do: if international reward points matter to your strategy, use this card for foreign spends before 25 October to catch the last of them. After that, budget for zero points on anything international and consider a co-branded card like the IndiGo one below, which is actually adding international rewards rather than removing them.

FIRST Classic

Same trade as FIRST Millennia above: zero forex markup goes live now, and international spends stop earning reward points from 26 October 2026. The birthday 10X bonus category also drops "international purchases" from its wording. Unverified from the bank's page. If you use this card mainly for domestic spends, nothing changes for you; for foreign spends, use it before 25 October if points matter, and expect zero after.

FIRST Select

Forex markup drops from 1.99% to 0%, with the same 26 October cutoff on international reward points. On ₹1 lakh of foreign spend, the old 1.99% (plus GST) markup cost roughly ₹2,340; at zero, you keep that. Losing reward points on the same ₹1 lakh (roughly 667 points at the base rate, worth ₹135 to ₹270) is a much smaller number by comparison.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: for international spend specifically, this is a clear net win once the fee drops, even after the points disappear in October. Just don't expect the points to keep coming.

FIRST Wealth

Forex markup drops from 1.5% to 0%, same 26 October cutoff on international reward points, and the birthday 10X bonus category quietly drops "international purchases," keeping only dining, travel, and your birthday-day spends.

On ₹3 lakh of annual foreign spend, a realistic number for a premium card like this, the old 1.5% (plus GST) markup cost roughly ₹5,310 a year; at zero, that's fully saved.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: the fee saving outweighs the lost points here too, but if birthday spending abroad was part of your 10X strategy on this card, that specific trick is gone from 26 October.

Ashva Metal Card

Forex markup drops from 1% to 0%, but unlike the cards above, Ashva doesn't zero out international rewards entirely. It cuts them from 5X to 2X, effective 26 October 2026, a 60% cut on that reward category regardless of the exact point value.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: Ashva remains one of the few IDFC FIRST cards that still rewards international spend after October, just less generously. Still worth using abroad ahead of a card that pays zero.

Business Credit Card (SME)

The low-interest variant's forex markup drops from 1.99% to zero, a genuine saving. But the high-reward variant's business-expense multiplier is cut from 10X to 4X, and the foreign-currency reward category itself, previously 5X on the low-interest variant and 10X on the high-reward variant, is removed from the card entirely.

A business spending ₹5 lakh a year in foreign currency on the high-reward variant used to earn at 10X on that spend; that category disappearing outright, stacked with the utility and advertising multiplier dropping from 10X to 4X, is a real reward cut sitting right next to the fee cut.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: if you run this card for foreign-currency business spends specifically, expect materially fewer points from today. The forex saving is real, but for high-volume business spends it's smaller in absolute terms than the reward cut.

IndiGo IDFC FIRST Dual Credit Card

Forex markup drops from 1.49% to 0%, matching every other card in this sweep. This one is the exception to the pattern though: from 26 October 2026, it will newly earn 1 IndiGo BluChip point for every ₹100 spent internationally, an addition, not a cut.

On ₹1 lakh of foreign spend, that's 1,000 BluChip points from October onward, on top of the roughly ₹1,760 in forex savings (1.49% plus GST on ₹1 lakh) you're already keeping today.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: of everything in today's IDFC FIRST sweep, this is the one card getting strictly better for international spend. Keep it for foreign travel bookings and BluChip accumulation.

FIRST Digital (Virtual UPI)

This card's UPI reward rate used to be a flat 3X on any UPI spend above ₹2,000, through any UPI app you used. From today, that 3X rate applies only when you pay through the IDFC FIRST Bank mobile app; pay the same amount through Google Pay, PhonePe, or any other UPI app, and you now earn just 1X. International spends on this card now earn zero rewards.

Spend ₹10,000 a month via UPI split across apps: if you were doing it all through a non-IDFC app, your reward rate on that spend just fell from 3X to 1X, a two-thirds cut, unless you switch your UPI app of choice to IDFC FIRST's own.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page.

What I'd do: if you use this card for UPI regularly, the free lunch just ended unless you're willing to route your scan-and-pay through IDFC FIRST's own app. If you won't switch apps, this card's value just dropped meaningfully.

FIRST SWYP

Zero forex markup joins this card too, but the bigger story is the welcome offer. The old bundle included an Amazon voucher worth ₹500, reward points worth ₹250 on your first EMI transaction, up to ₹500 off flights or hotels above ₹5,000 spend once a month, and ₹2,100 worth of EaseMyTrip discount coupons. All of that is gone, replaced with a flat ₹500 gift voucher on ₹5,000 of spend within 30 days.

Add up the old stack: ₹500 Amazon voucher, ₹250 in reward points, potentially ₹500 a month in travel discounts, and ₹2,100 in EaseMyTrip coupons; a new cardholder could plausibly have banked ₹3,000 or more in the first month or two. The new offer is worth ₹500, full stop.

The catch: unverified from the bank's page; this only affects new applicants, existing cardholders keep whatever they already earned.

What I'd do: if you were eyeing this card mainly for the welcome stack, that incentive just shrank by roughly 80%. Reconsider whether the everyday reward rate alone still makes this the right pick for you.

LIC Select

Joins the same zero forex markup update as the cards above; no other reward or fee change detected today. Unverified from the bank's page. If you hold this card, there's nothing to act on; the forex saving is a straightforward bonus with no catch attached.

LIC Classic

Same update as LIC Select: zero forex markup added, no other changes detected today. Unverified from the bank's page.

FIRST EA₹N

Zero forex markup added to this entry-level RuPay card; joining offer and fee structure otherwise unchanged. Unverified from the bank's page.

FIRST Power+

Zero forex markup now listed for this fuel co-branded card, with no other change detected today. Unverified from the bank's page.

Quantum+ Credit Card

Zero forex markup added; no other change detected today. Unverified from the bank's page.

Corporate Credit Card

This is the page carrying the umbrella line itself: "All IDFC FIRST Bank Credit cards now come with Zero forex markup." That confirms today's sweep across fourteen cards is a deliberate, bank-wide policy change, not a coincidence of separate page edits. Unverified from the bank's page; no press release seen yet.

What I'd actually do with this

If you hold an IDFC FIRST Bank card, don't panic and don't celebrate either. The zero forex markup is real money in your pocket starting today, and for most people it comfortably outweighs the reward points quietly disappearing on international spends from 26 October. The two exceptions worth acting on: if you use FIRST Digital for UPI, switch your payments to the IDFC FIRST Bank app itself or accept a two-thirds cut in your reward rate; and if you were applying for FIRST SWYP mainly for its welcome offer, that offer just lost roughly 80% of its value, so weigh the everyday card on its own merits now.

If you use the Axis Bank REWARDS card for rent or wallet top-ups, check whether the new 1% fee is costing you more than the card earns you back, and if it is, move that specific spend elsewhere.

If you or someone in your family earns ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 a month and travels by train, the HDFC IRCTC card just became reachable; there's no reason to wait to apply.

If you hold either of the two Kotak cards mentioned today, no urgent action is needed, just note the international reward cut on Royale Signature and the higher redemption bar on Cashback+ from mid-October.

This is my honest read of what these bank pages show today, not formal financial advice. I'm not your advisor, and before you make any big card decision, especially around business spends or a welcome offer you were counting on, run it past what actually fits your own spending pattern. But here's exactly how I'd think about it.
